analysis.one_liner: Auctions a shrinking cap on carbon permits and sends the money back to Americans as equal dividends.
analysis.headline: Senator Van Hollen's carbon cap-and-dividend bill died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors and never received a vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that sell oil, coal, and natural gas in the United States to buy carbon permits at government auctions, with the number of permits shrinking each year until 2050, when emissions would be capped 80% below 2005 levels. Every dollar raised would be divided evenly among lawful U.S. residents as a quarterly 'Healthy Climate Dividend.' A border fee would keep imported steel, cement, and other carbon-intensive goods from undercutting American manufacturers, and the EPA would have to regulate non-carbon greenhouse gases within ten years.
analysis.who_benefits: Every lawful U.S. resident with a valid Social Security number would receive an equal quarterly dividend funded entirely by the fossil fuel permit auctions, tax-free. Lower- and middle-income households, which spend a smaller share of income on fuel than wealthier households, would generally receive more in dividends than they pay in higher fuel prices. U.S. manufacturers of steel, aluminum, cement, and similar goods would be protected from imports made under weaker climate rules.

how_it_helps.text: Auction proceeds and penalties are deposited in a Healthy Climate Trust Fund and paid out as equal, tax-free quarterly dividends to every eligible individual, with opt-out allowed [S3].
The permit cap starts 12.5% below 2005 emissions in 2019 and declines on a fixed schedule to 80% below 2005 levels by 2050, giving companies a predictable, binding path to cut carbon pollution [S3].

Border fees on carbon-intensive imports (steel, aluminum, cement, glass, paper, chemicals) and rebates for U.S. exporters keep domestic manufacturers from being undercut by countries without equivalent carbon rules [S3].
The EPA must regulate all non-auction greenhouse gases within ten years, with citizen suits available to enforce the deadlines [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mines, oil refiners and petroleum importers, and natural gas suppliers would bear the direct cost of buying permits, a cost they would largely pass to consumers in fuel and energy prices; most households would get the money back through the dividend, but the largest fossil fuel producers and heaviest fossil fuel users would pay more than they receive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies

drawbacks.text: The permit requirement would raise prices for gasoline, home heating, and electricity, and households that drive long distances or heat large homes could pay more in fuel costs than they receive in dividends; the bill's design presumes the dividend outweighs this for most people, but heavy fuel users would lose [S3].
The bill exempts gases from the production of animals for food from EPA regulation, leaving a significant emissions source out of the program [S3].

Verifying that every dividend recipient is 'lawfully present' each quarter would require identity checks through the Social Security Administration and Treasury, adding a new administrative burden and data-sharing system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a deliberately simple version of carbon pricing: a hard, declining cap with all revenue returned equally to the public rather than spent by government or given to industry as free allowances. Its main real cost is higher fossil fuel prices, which the equal dividend offsets for most households but not for the heaviest fuel users. Its main weaknesses are the agricultural emissions carve-out and reliance on border adjustments that other trading partners could challenge.

outcome.mechanism: Van Hollen introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it; no cosponsor joined and the Congress ended before any vote.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) introduced the bill on January 29, 2018, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S1][S5].
No cosponsor ever joined the bill [S4].

The Finance Committee took no further action; the bill's action history after referral is empty, and the 115th Congress ended January 3, 2019, without a committee vote, hearing record, or floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies were better off because the bill never advanced, avoiding a permit-purchase mandate and a declining cap on their sales; no group gained in any other way, since the bill simply died without opposition being recorded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel companies that avoided permit costs

for.name: Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks; it was his Senate floor statement and referral that was the bill's only recorded action [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill on January 29, 2018 and took no further action — no markup, hearing, or vote — before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill and the majority never scheduled it for committee or floor action during the Congress [S4].

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so it never reached the point where a partisan split could be measured [S4][S5].

industries.note: Coal mines and coal importers would have had to buy permits for every ton of CO2 their fuel would emit, the highest per-energy carbon cost of any covered fuel, making coal the most exposed industry under the declining cap [S3].

Refineries and petroleum product importers would face annual permit auctions covering the emissions from the crude oil and petroleum products they sell, a new multibillion-dollar annual cost passed on at the pump [S3].
Gas deliverers and processors would buy permits for the CO2 content of gas sold to end users, though at a lower cost per unit of energy than coal or oil [S3].

industries.industry: U.S. steel, cement, aluminum, glass, paper, and chemical manufacturers
industries.note: Border fees on carbon-intensive imports and rebate payments to exporters would shield these energy-intensive manufacturers from competitors in countries without carbon rules [S3].

industries.industry: Renewable energy and energy efficiency industries
industries.note: A shrinking cap on fossil fuels with rising permit prices would steadily improve the relative economics of wind, solar, storage, and efficiency against oil, coal, and gas.
